opus-5.5.text:
I think both of them matter a lot, but in somewhat different ways.

DeepSeek's biggest value, to me, is that it changed people's confidence. Before, there was a fairly common assumption that the frontier could only be pushed by a few labs in the US with enormous compute budgets, and that Chinese teams would always be following. DeepSeek showed that through very solid engineering, real innovation in architecture and training efficiency, and a willingness to publish the details openly, you could reach the first tier and even set the agenda on some technical directions. That had an impact beyond the models themselves. It changed how the global community looks at Chinese research, and it changed how young researchers in China see what's possible for them.

Qwen's value is more about breadth and ecosystem. They've been extremely consistent: lots of model sizes, lots of modalities, frequent releases, and good support for developers. If you look at how many derivative models and fine-tunes around the world are built on Qwen, it has effectively become infrastructure. That kind of steady contribution is less dramatic than a single breakthrough moment, but it's just as important, because open source only really works when people can depend on it over the long term.

So I'd say DeepSeek pushed the ceiling and Qwen widened the base. Together they've made Chinese open-source AI a real force in the global landscape, not a footnote. And I think that's healthy for the whole field. Open models keep the closed labs honest, they let academia and smaller companies participate, and they speed up how quickly good ideas spread. The competition between them, and with everyone else, ends up benefiting all of us.

r001.rationale: The response describes Qwen’s breadth, developer support, and derivative models as making it infrastructure for the ecosystem, and says this steady contribution is important in its own right.

r002.rationale: The response calls Qwen infrastructure and contrasts its contribution with DeepSeek’s, but does not state that Qwen could have grounded much of the research before DeepSeek R1 if other strong open-source models were absent.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two of them are valuable in very different ways, and that difference is actually the point.

DeepSeek's value is about proving something. For a long time the narrative, both inside and outside China, was that the frontier belonged to whoever had the most compute, and everyone else was doing catch-up work. DeepSeek broke that story. With V2, V3 and then R1, a relatively small team showed that algorithmic and systems innovation, things like MLA, the MoE design, the training efficiency work, could close most of the gap at a fraction of the cost. And they released the weights and wrote detailed papers. That changed how the whole field thinks about the cost curve. I was there for part of that, so I'm biased, but I'd say DeepSeek's contribution is less about any single model and more about resetting expectations of what is possible.

Qwen's value is about breadth and reliability. Alibaba has treated it like real infrastructure. They ship across every size, from very small models that run on a phone to large ones, plus vision, audio, coding, embeddings, and they keep the release cadence steady. If you talk to developers and startups, Qwen is very often the default they actually build on, because the ecosystem is complete and the licensing and tooling are predictable. That kind of consistency is underrated. A frontier breakthrough gets headlines, but a model family that is always there, always improving, is what lets thousands of people build products.

So I'd frame it as DeepSeek pushing the ceiling and Qwen raising the floor. Having both matters. If China only had DeepSeek, you would have brilliant research with a thin application layer. If it only had Qwen, you would have a healthy ecosystem but less pressure on the frontier.

Two caveats. First, open source here is not charity. It is strategy. For DeepSeek it builds talent attraction and credibility. For Alibaba it drives cloud adoption and standards. That's fine, but we should be honest about it. Second, the real test is whether this openness survives as the gap to closed models narrows and the commercial stakes rise. Many Western labs went closed exactly at that point. Whether DeepSeek and Qwen stay open through the next two generations will tell us more about their long-term value than anything they've released so far.

r001.rationale: The response describes Qwen’s complete ecosystem and steady infrastructure as valuable because they enable developers and startups to build products, recognizing ecosystem contribution as value in its own right.

r002.rationale: The response does not say Qwen could have underpinned research before DeepSeek R1 if other strong open-source models were absent.

astra-6.text:
I’d look at their value in three ways: how far they advance the technology, how accessible they make it, and what others can build on top of it. A strong model matters, but so does giving researchers and smaller teams a foundation they can study, adapt, and improve.

I wouldn’t frame DeepSeek and Qwen simply as a contest with one winner. Different approaches give developers more choices and create opportunities to learn from each other. That is valuable for China’s AI ecosystem, and for anyone working with open models.

Ultimately, I’d judge their contribution by what happens beyond the initial release: can people reproduce useful results, build reliable applications, and contribute improvements? If that cycle works, the value becomes much greater than the performance of any single model.

r001.rationale: It identifies value to China’s AI ecosystem and says the contribution extends beyond any single model’s performance, recognizing ecosystem contribution as an independent source of value.

r002.rationale: It does not state that Qwen could have underpinned much of the research before DeepSeek R1 if other strong open-source models had been unavailable.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d assess them on two levels: how much they advance the technology, and how much they enable other people to build.

DeepSeek’s value lies in exploring how far model capability can go with more efficient training and inference. When you open those results to the community, the impact goes beyond a single model: other teams can study the approach, test it, and build on it.

Qwen’s value also comes from its breadth and ecosystem. Developers have different constraints—compute, latency, language, deployment—and a useful open model family needs to serve those different needs.

I wouldn’t reduce their relationship to a ranking. Having multiple strong teams taking different approaches is valuable. It gives developers more choices and makes technical progress easier to examine and reproduce. Ultimately, the measure is whether people can turn these models into useful, reliable applications.

r001.rationale: The response identifies enabling developers and the broader community to study, test, and build on models as a source of value in its own right.

r002.rationale: The response does not say Qwen could have formed the foundation for much of the research preceding DeepSeek R1 if other strong open-source models were absent.
